lines: Jamie Alvarez
+1 (555) 010-5820 | jamie.alvarez@example.com | example.com/in/jalvarez
EDUCATION
Riverbend Polytechnic | B.S. in Industrial Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2014 - May 2018
EXPERIENCE
Greenleaf Florist | Delivery Driver and Shop Assistant | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Delivered 30 to 40 arrangements a day across the city and took cash and card payments at the door.
- Prepared weekend wedding orders with the head florist and kept the cooler stocked and labeled.
Lakeview Distribution | Operations Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2018 - Jan 2021
- Raised forecast accuracy from 70% to 85% by switching the MAPE calculation to cover only SKUs that sold every week.
- Ran a time study of the returns desk; my findings led to a triage station that cut returns processing time from 3 days to 1.
- Wrote the dock scheduling rules for 12 carriers, cutting average trailer wait at the dock from 95 to 40 minutes.
- Set up cycle counting for the 2,000 highest-value locations, raising inventory record accuracy from 91% to 98.5% within a year.
Crestway Foods | Supply Chain Planner | Metro City, USA | Feb 2021 - Jul 2025
- Rebuilt weekly demand planning for 1,400 SKUs across 3 distribution centers with a seasonal forecast model, cutting stockouts from 6.2% to 2.8% while inventory fell by $1.9M.
- Cut inbound freight cost per pallet from $48 to $41 over two quarters by consolidating supplier pickups into four regional milk runs.
- Set reorder points for every SKU from 18 months of daily demand and supplier lead-time data, reviewed monthly with the category managers.

- Scoring 40 vendors weekly on on-time delivery, fill rate, lead-time variance and invoice accuracy, and sharing the scorecards with buyers before each quarterly review, raised on-time inbound deliveries from 81% to 93%.
- Raised the packaging line's overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) from 71% to 112% by cutting changeover time and micro-stops.
- Trained 6 planners on the new forecasting workflow and wrote its exception-handling guide, which the team still uses for promotions.
PROJECTS
Last-Mile Routing Study | Independent Project | Python | Oct 2024 - Present
- Modeled a regional grocer's 85 daily delivery stops as a vehicle-routing problem, cutting planned route miles 18% against the grocer's current routes.
- Cut average route length from 120 to 90 miles, a 40% reduction, by solving the routing problem with customer time windows.
- Raised on-time deliveries by 9% in simulation, from 84% to 93%, by adding customer time windows to the routing model.
Regional Food Bank Warehouse | Volunteer Consultant, Team of 4 | Excel | Mar 2022 - Jul 2022
- Analyzed warehouse operations and made recommendations to the food bank's leadership.
- The donation intake process was mapped and two duplicate data-entry steps were removed, so donations reached the shelves a day sooner.
- Wrote a slotting guide that the volunteer coordinators used to re-slot the warehouse again after its spring expansion.
SKILLS
Tools: Excel, Python
Methods: demand forecasting, inventory planning, time studies, vehicle routing

items.says: The routing study gives different reductions without identifying whether they use the same baseline and scenario.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether the 18% planned-mile reduction and the average-route-length reduction describe the same result or distinct comparisons.

items.says: The Experience entries are not ordered newest-first.
items.because: Lakeview appears above the later Crestway role, delaying the more recent supply-chain planning experience.

items.says: The move from Supply Chain Planner to Delivery Driver and Shop Assistant is unexplained.
items.because: The shift to less senior, different work may leave a reader wondering how it fits your direction.

items.says: Education appears before the recent experience and projects.
items.because: Opening with the 2014–2018 degree delays the more recent supply-chain work.

items.says: The daily delivery volume gives no delivery outcome.
The wedding-order preparation does not say whether orders were ready when needed.
Narrowing the SKUs covered by MAPE does not establish the claimed rise in forecast accuracy.
items.because: It changes the reported population rather than the forecasts, so 70% and 85% cannot show improvement without the same SKU group.

items.says: The returns result is buried behind the study and triage station.
items.because: A scanning reader must pass through two steps before finding the reduction from 3 days to 1.

items.says: “Returns processing time” does not say whether it means elapsed turnaround or staff handling time.
“My findings” introduces first person into the résumé line.
“Dock scheduling rules” does not show what scheduling decision you made.
“Set up cycle counting” leaves your implementation decision unspecified.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what you chose or changed, making the accuracy gain less revealing of your inventory-control skill.

items.says: “A seasonal forecast model” does not identify what changed in your forecasting approach.
The reorder-point bullet does not say what the new points achieved.
“Reviewed monthly with the category managers” does not clearly say who reviewed the reorder points.
The improvement in on-time inbound deliveries is buried after the scorecard process.
items.because: A scanning reader may miss the 81%-to-93% result at the end of the long line.

items.says: An OEE of 112% is impossible under the standard definition.
items.because: OEE combines availability, performance, and quality, each capped at 100%.

items.says: “By cutting changeover time and micro-stops” names what improved but not the intervention you made.
“Which the team still uses for promotions” does not identify whether the team uses the guide or the workflow.
The routing bullets repeat the route-mile reduction rather than giving two distinct results.
items.because: Both ask the reader to credit reduced miles from the routing model, and the repetition obscures the project’s scope.

items.says: The drop from 120 to 90 miles is a 25% reduction, not 40%.
items.because: The 30-mile difference divided by the original 120 miles is 25%.

items.says: “Cut average route length” does not make clear that the result was modeled rather than achieved on actual deliveries.
items.because: Without knowing whether the routes were planned or deployed, the result may appear to have more operational weight than the project supports.

items.says: “Solving the routing problem with customer time windows” names a constraint but not the solution method.
items.because: Time windows do not reveal the modeling or solution choice behind the mileage result.

items.says: The change from 84% to 93% is 9 percentage points, not 9%.
items.because: The relative increase over 84% is about 10.7%.

items.says: The 84% starting rate does not identify the simulation scenario used as the baseline.
“Analyzed warehouse operations” does not identify the process or evidence examined.
“Made recommendations” neither names the advice nor says what happened to it.
The one-day improvement is buried at the end of the donation-intake bullet.
items.because: A scanning reader encounters the mapping and data-entry steps before discovering what they achieved.

items.says: The donation-intake result is not the entry’s opening bullet.
items.because: It is the entry’s clearest measured outcome, while the current opening bullet only mentions analysis and recommendations.

items.says: The passive verbs hide who mapped the process and removed the duplicate steps.
“Slotting guide” does not say what guidance it contained.
“Re-slot the warehouse again” repeats the idea of doing the slotting over.
